question: Explain the belief in Tawheed.
answer: Belief in Tawheed (faith in the Oneness of Allah) is the first and most fundamental article of faith in Islam. The word "Tawheed" literally means to affirm oneness, while "Aqeedah" (derived from "Aqd", to tie fast) refers to the thoughts and ideas a person firmly believes in and which shape his character and attitudes. In Islamic terminology, Aqeedah-e-Tawheed means that the Creator, Owner and Sovereign of this universe is Allah Almighty alone, Who is from eternity and will last forever, with neither beginning nor end. He is the only God; He has created everything with perfect proportion and order. His knowledge encompasses every particle of the universe, He sees all, hears all, gives provisions, and guides. There is no precedent or example for Him; He is the owner of the gain and loss of creatures and the Giver of eternal life after death; He has no partner. To believe in this with firm conviction of the heart and to express it by the tongue when necessary is called Tawheed. It is the essence of all worship and the starting point of the call of every Prophet from Hazrat Adam to Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH), and the first part of the Kalima Tayyibah, "La ilaha illa Allah", reflects this very belief.
explanation: From the lesson's definitions of Aqeedah and Tawheed on page 65 (image 68); the belief is the first cardinal article of faith and the foundation of religion commanded by Allah and all the Prophets.

question: Write a detailed note on the requisite of Tawheed.
answer: The requisites (essential requirements) of Tawheed are those basic beliefs and practices without which the claim of believing in Allah Almighty becomes meaningless. First, Allah Almighty is unique and incomparable: "There is nothing like Him" (Surah Al-Shura: 11), so He must be believed in as an incomparable being. Second, there is only Allah Almighty whose pleasure man should seek. Third, all acts that fall into the category of worship must be reserved for Allah alone: prostration, vows and prayers should be kept for Him, supplications should be made to Him, refuge should be sought from Him, and only He should be called for help, as Allah says "Do not worship anyone other than Him" (Surah Al-Isra: 23). Fourth, all emotions and feelings in which the spirit of worship lies—praise and gratitude, hope and trust, fear and piety, true love and devotion, humility and submission—should be reserved for Allah Almighty alone. Fifth, the only sovereign of the whole universe is Allah; He alone has the right to command and forbid, He is the real Legislator, and He alone has the right to set the law of life, to forgive or to punish. Sixth, we should live this worldly life according to the guidance and commands sent by Allah Almighty, believing in Him with all His attributes. These requirements are so crucial that denying any of them makes the claim of believing in Allah meaningless; no one can be a true Muslim unless he believes in Tawheed with its full meaning.
explanation: Drawn from the "Requirements of Tawheed" section (pages 68-69, images 71-72), which lists uniqueness of Allah, exclusive worship, exclusive worship-emotions, exclusive sovereignty, and living by Allah's guidance.

question: What is the concept of faith (Iman)?
answer: Faith (Iman) rests on firm conviction of the heart. The word "Aqeedah" is derived from the Arabic "Aqd", meaning to tie fast, and refers to the thoughts and ideas a person firmly believes in, which affect his character and attitudes. Belief in Tawheed is the first cardinal article of faith in Islam, and a Muslim must first reform his belief before all else.
explanation: Based on the definition of Aqeedah and belief on page 65 (image 68).

question: What is meant by worship?
answer: Worship (Iba'dat) is to live according to the blessed life of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) with the intention of gaining the pleasure of Allah Almighty. It includes every action that Allah has commanded to do and abstaining from whatever He has forbidden, and it is the practical form of man's direct contact and relationship with Allah.
explanation: Based on the lesson's treatment of worship as the practical relationship with Allah (images 82-83).

question: Write a note on the effects of belief in Tawheed.
answer: When belief in Allah's oneness is firmly established in the heart, its beneficial effects appear in the personality and practical life. It develops love and respect for Allah, so the servant obeys His commands and avoids His prohibitions, attaining happiness in this world and the Hereafter. It gives man the highest position of freedom and liberty; creates piety, self-control and self-respect; creates humility; and makes him see all creatures with love and affection. It also gives man perseverance, courage, contentment, selflessness, determination, patience and trust by which he copes with life's difficulties, removes despair through belief in Allah's mercy, makes him fearless in doing Jihad to uplift the word of Allah, and creates the idea of the unity and equality of mankind.
explanation: Summarised from the "Effects of Aqeedah-e-Tawheed on Life" section (pages 69-70, images 72-73).

question: "Allah Almighty is eternal". Explain.
answer: Allah Almighty is eternal means He is "the First and the Last" (Surah al-Hadid: 3). Before there was anything, He existed alone, and in the end nothing will remain but He will remain alone. He has always been and will always be; He has neither beginning nor end, and no one has created Him. His attributes are eternal like His Being, and He is Al-Hayy (Ever-Living, Immortal).
explanation: From the first attribute of Allah, "Al-Awwal wal-Akhir" (Everlasting/Eternal), on page 67 (image 70).

question: What does the word "Tawheed" stand for?
answer: Literally, "Tawheed" stands for affirming oneness. In Islamic terminology it stands for the belief that Allah Almighty is One, unique, eternal and incomparable—the sole Creator, Owner and Sovereign of the universe, with no partner, no equal and no precedent—and to believe this with firm conviction of the heart and express it by the tongue when necessary.
explanation: Based on the literal and terminological meaning of Tawheed on page 65 (image 68).

question: Write down the literal and terminological meaning and concept of "Risaalat" and "Nubuwwat".
answer: "Nubuwwat" is derived from "Naba", which literally means news, and the one who gives news is called a "Nabi" (Prophet), whose plural is "Ambiyaa" (Prophets). "Risaalat" literally means to convey a message, and the one who conveys the message is called a "Rasool" (Messenger), whose plural is "Rusul" (Messengers). In religious terminology, Prophethood and Apostleship (Nubuwwat and Risaalat) is a high spiritual position on which Allah Almighty has appointed chosen servants from among His servants, through which man attains divine knowledge. It serves as a link between Allah Almighty and His servants: through it Allah conveys His commands and instructions to His servants, and through the Prophets He guides, corrects and trains human beings. The person who holds this position is called a Prophet or a Messenger; even before receiving the divine message, his status in his nation is very high—he is infallible, pious, gentle, virtuous, truthful and trustworthy. In Arabic, "Al-Rasool" specifically refers to the Messenger of Allah (PBUH), and it is obligatory to believe in all the Prophets and Messengers sent by Allah before him.
explanation: Directly from the section "The Literal and Terminological Meaning and Concept of Prophethood and Apostleship" (pages 71-72, images 74-75).

question: Write a note on the belief in Prophethood in detail.
answer: Belief in Prophethood (Nubuwwat) is the second most important and fundamental belief in Islam, and in the chain of Islamic beliefs it comes right after Tawheed (monotheism). It means to believe that Allah Almighty, out of His mercy, appointed chosen servants (Prophets and Messengers) to convey His guidance to mankind through divine revelation. The Holy Qur'an says: "They all believe in Allah, and His angels and His books and His messengers, and they say: We make no distinction among any of His messengers." (Surah Al-Baqarah: 285) Therefore, to believe in all the Prophets and Messengers sent by Allah Almighty before the Holy Prophet (PBUH) is obligatory. The need for Prophethood and Apostleship is evident from several points: (1) Islam states worship and obedience to Allah as the purpose of man's creation, which can occur only through the practical guidance of the Prophets and Messengers; (2) man naturally wants a practical example to mould his life, and the lives of the Prophets are the best practical example; (3) Allah reveals the Book on the Prophet for the guidance of His servants, and the Prophet teaches its teachings, commands and wisdom; (4) the Hereafter is a place of accountability, and without guidance people could plead ignorance on the Day of Resurrection; (5) just as Allah provided all facilities for man's physical needs, He blessed humanity with Prophetic guidance for its spiritual needs. Thus Prophethood is an essential link between Allah and His servants.
explanation: Based on the section "The need for Prophethood and Apostleship" (page 72, image 75) and the Qur'anic verse (Surah Al-Baqarah: 285).

question: Write a note on obedience and following The Holy Prophet (PBUH) in detail.
answer: The word "Ita'at" (obedience) is derived from "Tawun", which literally means heartfelt willingness and obedience. Obedience requires complete surrender; it does not accept obeying some commands while disobeying others. In other words, accepting obedience with a willing heart is called obedience. "Ittiba" (following one's footsteps) means to follow every step and every deed of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) with a deep heartfelt attachment and complete submission. When complete obedience and heartfelt love come together, it is called Ittiba. If someone obeys and follows the commands that the Holy Prophet (PBUH) has ordered or instructed, or his Sunnah in the matters of life, it is called following the footsteps of the Messenger of Allah. The main reason for ordering obedience to the Messenger is that Allah Almighty wants obedience to Him, and the only means of obedience to Allah is the Messenger, because Allah does not speak directly to His slaves but speaks through His Messengers. It is the Messenger who informs people about the instructions and commands of Allah. Therefore obedience to the Messenger is, in fact, obedience to Allah, and whoever wants to obey Allah must obey the Messenger of Allah. Without it, obedience to Allah cannot be imagined, as the Holy Qur'an says: "He who obeys the messenger of Allah, indeed he obeyed Allah." (Surah Al-Nisaa: 80)
explanation: Directly from the section "Obedience and Following to The Holy Prophet" (page 74, image 77), including the Qur'anic verse.

question: Explain the belief in the finality of Prophethood.
answer: The literal meaning of "Khat'm" is to seal, the end of something, and to finish by completing a task. Finality of Prophethood means that the series of Prophethood which started from Hazrat Adam (AS), with many Prophets coming one after another, ended with the Holy Prophet (PBUH). He is the last Prophet of Allah for all human beings till the Day of Resurrection, and now no new Prophet will come. Whoever claims Prophethood in any way after the Holy Prophet (PBUH) is an infidel and is out of the circle of Islam. The Holy Qur'an revealed to the Holy Prophet is the last eternal revelation of Allah to all humanity, after which no other book will be revealed. Allah Almighty says: "Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets" (Surah Al-Ahzab: 40), and He also says: "Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you, and I have chosen Islam as the religion for you." (Surah Al-Mai'dah: 3) The Holy Prophet (PBUH) said: "There will be among my Ummah thirty great liars, each of them asserting that he is (Allah's) prophet, whereas I am the Last Prophet. After me, there will be no Prophet." (Sunan Abu Dawood: 4252) Thus there is a unanimous consensus of the whole Ummah that the Holy Prophet (PBUH) is the Last Prophet of Allah.
explanation: From the sections "Finality of Prophethood" and "The need for the finality of Prophethood" (pages 75-76, images 76-77).

question: Describe the importance of the love for The Holy Prophet (PBUH) in Islam.
answer: In the light of the Holy Qur'an, there are four essential aspects of our relationship with the Holy Prophet (PBUH): faith, obedience, following his footsteps, and love. Love is the name of a natural attraction and passion, and when it is based on a religious relationship it is called "spiritual love" or "love of faith". The Holy Prophet (PBUH) deserves all kinds of love from us, and this is a requirement of faith because he is the beloved of Allah and the benefactor and mentor of the believers. Therefore Allah Almighty commands us to love His Messenger, and any faith or obedience not based on the love of the Messenger is not valid in the sight of Allah. The requisite of this love is that it should not be merely outward and formal, but a love that overcomes all other loves, in comparison to which even the dearest and most beloved relationship loses its value, and for which everything in the world can be sacrificed. This is the standard of love stated in the Holy Qur'an: "The Prophet has more rights for the believers than their own lives." (Surah Al-Ahzab: 6) In Hadith, the love of the Messenger of Allah is declared a sign of faith: "None of you can be a (true) believer unless he loves me more than his parents, children and all people." (Sahih Bukhari, Book of Iman, Hadith 15)
explanation: From the section "Love for The Holy Prophet" (page 73, image 76), including the Qur'anic and Hadith references.

question: Who is called a Prophet or a Messenger?
answer: The one who receives and gives the news of Allah is called a "Nabi" (Prophet), and the one who conveys the divine message is called a "Rasool" (Messenger). In religious terminology, the chosen servant appointed by Allah Almighty to the high spiritual position of Prophethood and Apostleship—through whom Allah conveys His commands and guidance to His servants—is called a Prophet or a Messenger.
explanation: Based on the definition given on page 71 (image 74).

question: Write down the characteristics of the Prophethood of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH).
answer: Prophethood started with Prophet Adam (AS) and came to an end on Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH), the Messenger of Allah and the last of all Prophets. The perfections which Allah Almighty bestowed on all previous Prophets individually, He blessed with all of them together in the Shari'ah of the Holy Prophet (PBUH). His Shari'ah has surpassing significance and comprises the excellencies of all previous Prophets' Shari'ahs. Its distinguishing features include generality and universality, abrogation of the first Shari'ah, perfection (preservation of the Divine Book), protection of the Sunnah of the Prophet, comprehensiveness, and finality of Prophethood.
explanation: From the section "Characteristics of the Prophethood of Muhammad" (pages 74-75, images 77-78).

question: What do the Holy Qur'an and Hadith guide us about the finality of Prophethood?
answer: The Holy Qur'an says: "Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets (Last of the Prophets)" (Surah Al-Ahzab: 40). The Holy Prophet (PBUH) said: "There will be among my Ummah thirty great liars, each of them asserting that he is (Allah's) prophet, whereas I am the Last Prophet. After me, there will be no Prophet." (Sunan Abu Dawood: 4252) Thus no Prophet will come after him, and there is a unanimous consensus of all the Ummah that the Holy Prophet (PBUH) is the Last Prophet of Allah.
explanation: From the Qur'anic verse and Hadith quoted in the section on the finality of Prophethood (page 76, image 77).

question: What is the sign of perfect faith? Write down.

The Holy Prophet (PBUH) said: "None of you can be a (true) believer unless he loves me more than his parents, children and all people." (Sahih Bukhari, Book of Iman, Hadith 15) Thus loving the Holy Prophet (PBUH) more than all other relationships is the sign of perfect faith.

question: Write a note on "Iba'dat" (worship) in detail.
answer: "Iba'dat" is an Arabic word derived from "Abd". Literally it means worship, humility, submission and obedience. In Islamic terminology, "Iba'dat" means to live according to the blessed life of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) with the intention of gaining the pleasure of Allah Almighty. It includes every action which Allah has commanded to do and abstaining from whatever He has forbidden. Since the servant's job is to obey the master—especially when He is the Master of all the rulers—to consider His commands as a cause of happiness and contentment for oneself is the ascension of a servant. In Islam, after the reformation of faith and belief, the first emphasis is given to worship, because worship is the practical form of direct contact and relationship with Allah Almighty. Allah Almighty says: "And I have not created Jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me." (Surah Al-Zariyat: 56) and "O people! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may save (from His punishment)." (Surah Al-Baqarah: 21) Here worship refers to piety, which is the destination after the purification of the heart and soul and sincerity of action; this condition of a man's heart leads to love for good deeds and hatred of evils.
explanation: From the sections "The meaning and concept of worship" and "The Importance and Significance of Worship" (pages 79-80, images 82-83).

question: Write down the effects of worship on general life.
answer: The Islamic system of worship develops feelings of love and sympathy in man for other human beings; therefore a Muslim loves, sympathizes with, and helps others in their sorrows. Worship also teaches patience and forbearance and awakens the spirit to sacrifice one's own interests for the sake of Allah Almighty and the collective good. It teaches man to live together collectively, so he learns to live with other human beings and becomes a socialist. The punctuality of worship eliminates bad habits like laziness, idleness and wastage of time, and creates in man the qualities of observance of time, outward and inward purification, obedience of a leader and collectivity, so that he abstains from evils and obscenities. Fasting creates piety in man—that is, the fear of Allah Almighty, which helps him distinguish between good and evil. Through paying Zakat the love of wealth decreases within man and he becomes happy to help others financially; Hajj teaches universality; and good deeds like helping people, relating with kin and caring for subordinates improve relationships and affiliations. The correctness of intention and sincerity are the keys to acceptance, and then every good deed has the status of worship for the believer.
explanation: From the section "Effects of Worship on Man's Practical Life" (pages 80-81, images 83-84).

question: Write down the importance and significance of worship.
answer: In Islam, the first emphasis, after the reformation of faith or belief, is given to worship. Worship is the practical form of direct contact and relationship with Allah Almighty, and it is the very purpose of man's creation. Allah Almighty says: "And I have not created Jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me." (Surah Al-Zariyat: 56) and "O people! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may save (from His punishment)." (Surah Al-Baqarah: 21) Every day in every prayer, Muslims repeatedly pray for the straight path, and the verse "And proclaim that my prayers, my sacrifices, and my life and death are all for Allah, the Lord of the worlds" (Surah al-Anaam: 162) gives a brief and comprehensive outline of the straight path, which is the soul of Islamic life and the lifeblood of Islamic society. This verse states that every Muslim's breath, step and deed should be for Allah Almighty's sake alone, not for the other or one's own desire—this is the purpose of a Muslim's life. Thus worship is the means of gaining the pleasure of Allah, of purifying the heart and soul, and of establishing piety, which is the destination of the believer.
explanation: From the sections on the concept and importance of worship (pages 79-80, images 82-83), including the Qur'anic verses cited.

Enter into Islam wholeheartedly." (Surah Al-Baqarah: 208) The correctness of intention and sincerity are also the keys to the acceptance of worship.
explanation: From the section "The Requisites of Worship" on page 80 (image 83).

question: Explain the significance and importance of Jihad.
answer: Islam has given much importance to Jihad because only through Jihad is it possible to create an atmosphere of peace and security in the world and to protect human rights by eliminating distortion, corruption, oppression and all kinds of evil deeds which cause conflict and disorder in society. Allah Almighty says: "And do Jihad in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives, it is better for you if you knew." (Surah Al-Tawbah: 41) Regarding the emphasis on Jihad, the Messenger of Allah (PBUH) said: "One who died in a state that he did not fight in the way of Allah practically nor did he express any desire (or determination) for Jihad, so he died the death of a hypocrite." (Sahih Muslim: 1910) Thus Jihad is a great duty that establishes peace, promotes goodness and virtue, eliminates evils and vices from society, protects human rights, and defends the religion, life, property and honour of the Muslims.
explanation: From the section "The significance and importance of Jihad" (page 82, image 85), including the Qur'anic verse and the Hadith.

question: Describe the types of Jihad.
answer: According to the lesson, the types of Jihad and its practical forms are three. (1) Jihad against the desires of the self: the inner strength that prevents man from obeying and worshipping Allah is the soul which enjoins evil and incites man to commit sins and disobedience, including selfishness, hatred, backbiting, lies, vulgar talking and other self-desires; the domination of these desires corrupts human actions and character. Overcoming this enjoin-er of evils falls into the category of Jihad. Allah says: "And for one who fears to stand before his Lord and restrains his soul from evil desire, then indeed Paradise only is his destination." (Surah al-Nazi'at: 40-41) The Holy Prophet (PBUH) declared a person who controls his self to be a Mujahid: "A Mujahid is one who strives against his own soul (regarding obedience to Allah)." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 1621) In some traditions, striving against one's soul is declared the biggest Jihad (Jihad-e-Akbar). (2) Jihad to eradicate evils: when individual evils prevail commonly in a society they take the form of collective evils, which Islam names Munkaraat. Islam not only rejects every action that causes trouble in society but commands believers to eradicate it, so that the social order remains peaceful and organized. The Prophet (PBUH) said: "He who sees something evil amongst you should change it with the help of his hand; and if he has not strength enough to do it, then he should do it with his tongue, and if he has not strength enough, then he should dislike it from his heart." (Sahih Muslim: 49) It is the responsibility of the government to eradicate evils with force, of the scholars and writers to forbid them with tongue and pen, and of every individual to consider evil as vicious and avoid it. The best Jihad is to speak a word of justice in front of a tyrant ruler (Sunan Abu Dawood: 4344). (3) Jihad by the sword / Armed Jihad (Fighting): if an enemy force invades an Islamic country, then it becomes obligatory on it to fight and protect its borders, religion, faith, life and property, and the honour and dignity of its citizens.
explanation: From the section "Types of Jihad and its Practical Forms" (pages 82-84, images 85-87), which enumerates jihad against the self, jihad to eradicate evils, and armed jihad.

question: Write down the conditions for Jihad.
answer: Islam has laid down certain conditions for armed Jihad which should be kept in view while doing Jihad. (A) For the exaltation of the religion of Allah: the first condition is that armed Jihad should be only for the exaltation of the religion of Allah. (B) Declaration by the Islamic State: the second condition is that the state should make a declaration of war; in Islam only the state has the authority to declare war, so the declaration of an individual or a group, or issuing a Fatwa, has no value in Shariah for waging war—rather such Fatwa or declarations fall into the category of mischief on earth. (C) Adequate availability of military power: the government should have adequate power and strength to fight the opposing force, and the Holy Qur'an emphasizes keeping the Islamic state strong: "Prepare (as much as possible) against them what you can of military power and cavalry to deter Allah's enemies and your enemies..." (Surah al-Anfaal: 60) The meaning is that Muslims should always be ready with the equipment of war and a permanent army to take immediate action in case of need and fight the enemy to the fullest. (D) Methods of ignorance should not be used in war: the fight should be against those who are armed in battle and ready to fight; women, children, the elderly, the wounded and civilians should not be attacked, and the victims of the enemies should not be cut off their ears and noses, nor should fields, houses and livestock be destroyed without any reason.
explanation: From the section "Conditions of armed Jihad" (pages 87-88, images 90-91).

question: What is the meaning and concept of Jihad?
answer: Jihad is an Arabic word derived from "Juh'd". It literally means hard work, striving hard, doing the utmost hard and endeavour. In Islamic Shariah, Jihad means to make every effort and endeavour for the sake of Allah Almighty, which is for the upliftment, protection and defence of the country and nation; and also every effort and endeavour for the reformation of society—to promote goodness and virtue and eliminate evils and vices from society.
explanation: From the section "Meaning and concept of Jihad" and its Shariah term (page 82, image 85).

question: Explain the objectives of Jihad.
answer: Besides defending and protecting the Islamic state, the Holy Qur'an describes other objectives of armed Jihad: (A) Punishment for breaking the agreement—Islam commands fighting against a nation that makes an agreement with the Islamic government not to wage war but has intentions of war behind that agreement, for Allah does not like the treacherous; the command is general though its background was a special occasion. (B) Respect for humanity and helping the oppressed—the Islamic government must support and help the oppressed and rid them of the oppressor's oppression, as stated in Surah Al-Nisa: 75 concerning oppressed men, women and children. (C) Elimination of sedition and mischief—wherever a government or group attacks the weak for its evil purposes and inflicts oppression and mischief, the Qur'an urges the Islamic State to wage war against them until there is no more persecution and the religion is entirely for Allah (Surah al-Baqarah: 193).
explanation: From the section "The objectives of the armed Jihad" (pages 86-87, images 89-90).
